prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Light Field Microscopy (LFM) allows for snapshot 3D imaging, but it faces a critical bottleneck in live-cell applications: the trade-off between exposure time and sensor noise. To capture dynamic processes, exposure times must be short, resulting in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) images. Current reconstruction algorithms fail under these conditions; they either require ground-truth 3D data (which is practically impossible to obtain for dynamic biological samples) or they implicitly average noise, leading to artifacts and blurring. Furthermore, standard self-supervised denoising techniques (like Noise-to-Noise) cannot be directly applied to LFM because the input views are not pixel-wise aligned—they are distinct angular projections where coordinate matching is physically impossible without prior reconstruction. We need a framework that can jointly denoise and reconstruct 3D volumes without requiring clean reference data.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the principle of "Noise-to-Noise" learning can be adapted to the 3D reconstruction domain by exploiting the redundancy across angular views. Our core hypothesis is that while sensor noise is independent across different light field views, the underlying 3D biological signal is consistent. By partitioning the available views into non-overlapping subsets and forcing a network to predict one subset from the other via a physics-based projection, we can compel the model to learn the consistent signal while discarding the random noise. Additionally, we hypothesize that standard convolutional networks fail to capture high-frequency details because they lack physical context; incorporating wave-optics priors directly into the feature alignment process will significantly improve detail recovery.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We aim to build a "View-to-View" (V2V) unsupervised learning framework. The approach mimics a simulation-based design process:

1.  **View Partitioning Strategy:** Instead of using all angular views simultaneously for reconstruction, we will split the raw input views into two disjoint subsets. In each training iteration, one subset will serve as the input to the reconstruction network, while the other subset acts as the supervision target.
2.  **Physics-Informed Re-projection Loop:**
    *   The network will take the noisy input subset and predict a 3D intensity volume.
    *   To calculate loss, we will not compare this 3D volume to a ground truth (which doesn't exist). Instead, we will use the physical forward model (the optical Point Spread Function or PSF) to mathematically project this predicted 3D volume onto the angles of the *held-out* supervision subset.
    *   The loss is calculated between these "simulated" views and the "real" noisy views of the supervision subset. Since the noise in the input and target is independent, the network converges to the clean signal.
3.  **Wave-Optics Feature Alignment:** To handle the complex geometry of light rays, we will design a custom feature alignment module within the encoder.
    *   Standard back-projection acts as a low-pass filter, blurring features.
    *   We propose to transform the theoretical PSF into sharpened convolution kernels.
    *   These kernels will be used to "warp" or back-project 2D feature maps from individual views into a unified 3D feature space. This ensures that features from different angles are spatially aligned before they are fused by the decoder.
4.  **Spectral and Consistency Constraints:** We will employ a loss function that operates in both the spatial and frequency domains (using Fourier transforms) to prevent the over-smoothing of high-frequency textures. We also plan to introduce a regularization term to suppress "crosstalk" artifacts, penalizing intensities that fall below the sensor's background noise floor.

## Expected Contribution
This research expects to deliver a robust, unsupervised solution for 3D fluorescence microscopy in low-light conditions. Theoretically, it extends self-supervised denoising principles to non-aligned multi-view geometry, offering a novel way to handle view-dependent signal consistencies. Practically, this will enable high-speed, long-duration imaging of sensitive biological specimens without phototoxicity, recovering high-resolution details that are currently lost to sensor noise in standard reconstruction pipelines.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive experimental framework to evaluate the proposed view-to-view denoised 3D reconstruction method (V2V3D) against existing state-of-the-art techniques.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Synthetic Dataset:** We simulated light field imaging using the principle of Two-Photon Synthetic Aperture Microscopy (2pSAM). We generated 1618 high-SNR 3D intensity volumes ($512 \times 512 \times 39$ resolution) from six biological scenarios: B cells, dendrites, microglia, neurons, neutrophils, and blood vessels. Physics-based forward projection generated 13 views ($512 \times 512 \times 13$) per volume. Substantial Gaussian noise was added to simulate real imaging. The test set consisted of 11 typical cases.
    *   **Real-world Dataset:** Acquired using a 2pSAM system. We captured thick samples with shortened exposure times to induce low SNR. Samples included one static sample (mouse brain slice, 100 frames) and one live sample (neutrophils, 100 frames). Each frame had a resolution of $512 \times 512 \times 13$.
    *   **Macro-scale Dataset:** We adapted the "Fern" scene from the LLFF dataset. Views were sub-sampled by a factor of 4, and severe Gaussian noise ($\mu=0, \sigma=50$) was added.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR):** Used to measure reconstruction accuracy.
    *   **Structural Similarity Index (SSIM):** Used to measure structural similarity.
    *   **Runtime (s):** Elapsed time for reconstruction.
    *   **Parameters (M):** Number of model parameters in millions.
    *   *Note:* Background noise was subtracted from reconstruction results and ground truth before metric calculation.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **RLD:** Richardson-Lucy Deconvolution (optimization-based).
    *   **VCDNet:** Supervised-learning-based convolutional network (retrained on our dataset using noisy LFIs as input and noise-free 3D signal as supervision).
    *   **DINER:** NeRF-based method (unsupervised).
    *   **DeepCAD+RLD:** DeepCAD used for pre-denoising LFIs, followed by RLD reconstruction.
    *   **DeepCAD+DINER:** DeepCAD used for pre-denoising LFIs, followed by DINER reconstruction.
    *   **IBRNet:** Used as a baseline for the macro-scale validation (both pre-trained and fine-tuned versions).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** Computations were performed on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.
    *   **Loss Functions:** The total loss included MSE loss, FFT loss (weight $\alpha = 0.1$), and De-crosstalk loss (weight $\beta = 1$).
    *   **Architecture:** The framework utilized two branches, each with a pyramid encoder (weights shared), a wave-optics-based feature alignment module, a U-Net-based decoder, and a physics-based forward projection module.
    *   **View Splitting:** The 13 views were divided into two non-overlapping subsets (odd and even) for the view-to-view self-supervision strategy.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Noise Handling on Synthetic Data:** We observed that pre-denoising with DeepCAD improved the performance of RLD and DINER but introduced artifacts. Our method achieved higher PSNR without separate pre-denoising steps, effectively recovering high-resolution, high-SNR 3D signals from severe noise.
*   **Comparison with Supervised Methods:** While VCDNet (supervised) effectively mitigated noise, it failed to reconstruct high-frequency details as effectively as our method, likely due to the lack of physics-informed feature alignment.
*   **Real-world Static Samples (Dendrites):**
    *   We obtained a high-SNR reference center view via time averaging.
    *   RLD and DINER reconstructions exhibited significant deficiencies, treating noise as valid signal.
    *   VCDNet produced noticeable artifacts due to poor generalization to real-world data distributions.
    *   Pre-denoising with DeepCAD caused signal crosstalk and blurring in the baselines.
    *   Our method consistently separated valid signals from noise, producing clearer reconstructions.
*   **Real-world Live Samples (Neutrophils):**
    *   DeepCAD was used to generate a reference center view for this dynamic sample.
    *   Consistent with static results, baselines suffered from artifacts and noise retention, while our method preserved details and removed noise.
*   **Macro-scale Scenario (Fern):**
    *   We validated the method on a noisy "Fern" scene.
    *   The PSNR values observed were: IBRNet (23.02), IBRNet-finetune (23.35), and Ours (25.87).
    *   Our method visually and quantitatively outperformed both pre-trained and fine-tuned IBRNet models on the noisy macro images.
*   **Ablation Analysis:**
    *   **V2V Framework:** Removing the view-to-view framework caused a substantial performance drop (PSNR from 39.05 to 30.81), confirming its critical role in denoising.
    *   **Feature Alignment:** Removing the wave-optics-based feature alignment led to a loss of detail and image sharpness.
    *   **De-crosstalk Loss:** Excluding this loss significantly increased artifacts caused by signal crosstalk along the Z-axis.
    *   **Fusion Strategy:** We tested other fusion strategies (max-pooling, learnable aggregation) but found no significant improvement over the averaging approach used in the final model.

prompt.name: SYSTEM.md
prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables
```latex
\begin{table}
  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
    \toprule
    Method & Frobnability \\
    \midrule
    Theirs & Frumpy \\
    Yours & Frobbly \\
    Ours & Makes one's heart Frob\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \caption{Results.   Ours is better.}
  \label{tab:example}
\end{table}
```

## Example Code for Figures
```latex

  \centering
  \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{0.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
   %\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{egfigure.eps}

   \caption{Example of caption.
   It is set in Roman so that mathematics (always set in Roman: $B \sin A = A \sin B$) may be included without an ugly clash.}
   \label{fig:onecol}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure*}
  \centering
  \begin{subfigure}{0.68\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{An example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-a}
  \end{subfigure}
  \hfill
  \begin{subfigure}{0.28\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{Another example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}
\end{figure*}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Light Field Microscopy (LFM) offers unparalleled capabilities for capturing snapshot-based, large-scale 3D fluorescence images. However, a critical bottleneck exists in reconstructing high-fidelity volumetric data from these captures, particularly under the gentle imaging conditions required for live-cell microscopy. These low-light environments result in substantial sensor noise.

Existing reconstruction algorithms face a dilemma:
1.  **Optimization-based methods (e.g., Richardson-Lucy Deconvolution):** These are computationally expensive and iteratively update volumes based on Poisson assumptions, which implicitly averages noise across views, leading to artifacts and smoothing rather than true denoising.
2.  **Supervised Deep Learning:** These require ground-truth 3D volumetric data, which is practically impossible to obtain for dynamic biological processes.
3.  **Standard Noise-to-Noise (N2N) methods:** While N2N works for 2D images by mapping between independent noisy realizations, it fails in LFM because individual light field views possess parallax (coordinate mismatch). The 2D coordinates of photons from the same 3D point differ across views, breaking the pixel-wise correspondence required for standard N2N.

We aim to resolve the conflict between the need for high-resolution 3D reconstruction and the lack of clean, paired training data in noisy, snapshot scenarios.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose **V2V3D**, a view-to-view based framework that unifies image denoising and 3D reconstruction into a single unsupervised architecture.

Our core hypothesis is that while noise in each Light Field (LF) view is independent, the views are derived from a consistent underlying 3D signal. By partitioning the angular views into non-overlapping subsets, we can train a network to predict the views of one subset using the information from the other. This enforces the network to learn the consistent 3D structure while ignoring the independent noise, effectively effectively applying the Noise-to-Noise principle to non-coordinate-matched light field data.

Furthermore, we hypothesize that standard convolutional networks struggle with LF data because they lack physical priors regarding the optical point spread function (PSF). We propose a **wave-optics-based feature alignment** technique that transforms physical PSFs into convolution kernels. This will allow us to warp features from 2D view space into a unified 3D space without the blurring effects typically associated with back-projection, thereby recovering high-frequency details.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Mathematical Modeling of LFM Formation
We will model the light propagation using wave optics. We define the direction of propagation as the $\mathsf{Z}$-axis. The 3D sample volume is discretized into points with intensity $I_{x,y,z}$. The system consists of $U$ beams (views) modeled by their respective Point Spread Functions, $PSF_{u,x,y,z}$. The captured Light Field Image (LFI) for a specific view $u$ is formulated as:

$$ L F I _ { u , x , y } = { \sum } _ { z } ( I _ { x , y , z } * P S F _ { u , x , y , z } ) $$

where $*$ denotes the 2D convolution operation.

### 2. View-to-View Self-Supervised Framework
To enable denoising without ground truth, we will divide the total available views $U$ into two non-overlapping subsets, $U_1$ and $U_2$. We will employ two reconstruction networks (sharing weights in the encoder) to generate 3D volumes from these subsets.

The training objective is to predict the views in subset $U_2$ using the volume reconstructed from subset $U_1$ (and vice versa). Specifically, the simulated view $u_2 \in U_2$ will be generated as follows:

$$ L \hat { F } I _ { u _ { 2 } , x , y } = \sum _ { z } ( f ( L F I _ { U _ { 1 } , x , y } ) * P S F _ { u _ { 2 } , x , y , z } ) $$

Here, $f(\cdot)$ represents the U-Net-based reconstruction network that estimates the 3D intensity volume $\hat{I}_{x,y,z}$ from the input subset. This creates a disjoint input/output pairing, preventing identity mapping and forcing the network to converge to the statistical expectation of the signal, effectively removing zero-mean independent noise.

### 3. Wave-Optics-Based Feature Alignment
Standard concatenation of views into CNN channels fails to handle the intensity variations caused by the angular disparity. We will implement a specialized Feature Alignment Module.

Inspired by Richardson-Lucy back-projection, we want to warp feature maps into 3D space. However, directly using the inverse PSF ($PSF^{-1}$) acts as a low-pass filter, blurring features. Instead, we will construct a sparse kernel $Kernel_{PSF^{-1}}$:
1.  Compute the centroid coordinates of each slice of the physical PSF.
2.  Set centroid positions to 1 and all other positions to 0 (effectively a Dirac delta function at the optical correspondence).
3.  The inverse kernel is defined by spatial flipping: $PSF_{u,x,y,z}^{-1} = PSF_{u,-x,-y,z}$.

The feature alignment operation for the network intermediate layers is then defined as:

$$ F e a t u r e _ { a l i g n } = F e a t u r e * K e r n e l _ { P S F ^ { - 1 } } $$

This aligns features from different angular views into a unified 3D coordinate system, enabling the subsequent 3D convolutional layers to aggregate information effectively without blurring high-frequency details.

### 4. Network Architecture
The pipeline will consist of two symmetric branches. Each branch includes:
1.  **Encoder:** A pyramid structure for multi-scale feature extraction.
2.  **Alignment Module:** The proposed wave-optics kernel projection described above.
3.  **Decoder:** A U-Net architecture generating the 3D volume.
4.  **Forward Projector:** A physics-based module implementing Eq. 1 to generate supervision views.

The final inference output will be the average of the 3D volumes generated by both branches.

### 5. Loss Functions
To ensure structural fidelity and high-frequency recovery, we will utilize a composite loss function $L_{all}$.

**A. MSE Loss:**
$$ L _ { M S E } = \frac { \sum _ { i } ( L F I _ { i } - L \hat { F } I _ { i } ) ^ { 2 } } { N } $$

**B. FFT Loss:**
To combat the over-smoothing common in LFM reconstruction (due to defocus), we will minimize the difference in the frequency domain:
$$ L _ { F F T } = \frac { \left. F F T ( L F I ) - F F T ( L \hat { F } I ) \right. _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } { N } $$

**C. De-crosstalk Loss:**
LFM often suffers from "crosstalk" where high-intensity signals bleed into dark areas along the Z-axis. We will enforce a sparsity constraint that penalizes intensity values falling below the estimated background noise level ($BG$):
$$ L _ { D C } = \sum _ { x , y , z } R e L U ( B G - \hat { I } _ { x , y , z } ) $$

**Total Loss:**
We will optimize the following weighted sum, tentatively setting $\alpha = 0.1$ and $\beta = 1$:
$$ L _ { a l l } = L _ { M S E } + \alpha L _ { F F T } + \beta L _ { D C } $$

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Unsupervised Paradigm Shift:** We will establish V2V3D as the first framework to successfully adapt Noise-to-Noise principles to Light Field Microscopy, enabling simultaneous denoising and reconstruction without ground-truth volumes or pre-denoising steps.
2.  **Physical-Feature Integration:** The proposal of transforming physical PSF priors into binary convolution kernels for feature alignment is a theoretical novelty that addresses the specific challenge of preserving high-frequency details in deep learning-based optical reconstruction.
3.  **Robustness to Noise:** By mathematically decoupling the noise realizations of split views, the architecture is expected to provide superior reconstruction quality in low-SNR conditions compared to methods that average noise (RLD) or rely on temporal consistency.

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
